title: Personal Design and Motion — The Slow and the Snappy

segments.text: This is Personal Design and Motion, late and low-lit. Something odd sits on your shelf tonight: a pile of people who worship fast, snappy motion, and one quiet note of your own that wants the opposite.
You wrote your own law for how a site should feel. Listen to what you asked motion to actually do.
Motion should feel physical and slow to settle: text revealing line by line as you scroll, images that open up instead of fading in, sections that pin while something changes.
segments.speaker: you, in your own note

segments.text: Now hear Emil Kowalski, saved right beside you, almost arguing back.
Fast animations improve the perceived performance.
segments.speaker: Emil Kowalski

segments.text: Snappy animations feel responsive and connected to user's actions.
segments.speaker: Emil Kowalski

segments.text: So who's right? Maybe both. His fast is for buttons you hit all day. Your slow is for a page someone visits once, and should feel.
Here's where they secretly agree. Emil's real enemy was never slowness. It's the instant.
Changes in web apps often occur instantly, which makes the experience feel artificial and unfamiliar, since nothing in world around us disappears or appears instantly.
segments.speaker: Emil Kowalski

segments.text: And the Chrome scroll note, two shelves over, quietly hands you the cure: tie the motion to something real, your own scroll.
A scroll-driven animation is linked to the scroll position of a scroll container. This means that as you scroll up or down, the linked animation scrubs forward or backward in direct response.
segments.speaker: Bramus, developer.chrome.com

source.title: Animate elements on scroll with Scroll-driven animations

segments.text: That's your word, physical, in one sentence. Your hand moves, the image moves. Nothing appears from nowhere.
Last one, the thing you probably wouldn't notice. All this beauty is really a performance trick wearing a nice coat.
you should try to animate with transform and opacity as they only trigger the third rendering step (composite), while padding or margin triggers all three (layout, paint, composite).
segments.speaker: Emil Kowalski

segments.text: And Chrome says the very same thing from the other direction.
you can now have silky smooth animations, driven by scroll, running off the main thread, with just a few lines of extra code.
segments.speaker: Bramus, developer.chrome.com

source.title: Animate elements on scroll with Scroll-driven animations

segments.text: The elegance you admire on those award pages is partly just work the browser was spared. The calm is engineering.
So carry this into your next build: which moments deserve your slow, physical settle, and which should snap and get out of the way? Sleep on that. This was Personal Design and Motion. Goodnight.
